newsitem.title: CONGO: U.S. Marines fly out of Congo after Zaire watch.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Marines fly out of Congo after Zaire watch.

text.p: United States marines flew out of the Congo capital Brazzaville on Monday as they stepped down their mission to pluck expatriates to safety from neighbouring Zaire in case of a feared bloodbath.

Hercules transport planes left Brazzaville with the first groups of around 200 marines for Congo's port of Pointe Noire where they were to transfer by helicopter to the amphibious assault ship USS Kearsage, off the Atlantic Coast.

"Around 150 men will stay around here for the moment, but things seem very quiet over there (in Zaire). If it stays the same then we may all be gone in a couple of days," force spokesman Commander Bob Anderson told Reuters.
"The present pullback means we would be able to respond within 12 hours instead of 60 minutes if there was trouble."

Laurent Kabila's rebels at the weekend captured Zaire's capital Kinshasa after a seven-month war to overthrow President Mobutu Sese Seko, who dominated the anarchic country at the heart of Africa for more than three decades.
At least 200 people were reported killed in violence in the teeming city of five million but the Americans, from one of five Western states with troops in Brazzaville, were never ordered into action.
"I guess it's quite good things didn't get bad over there for the people in Kinshasa. Our presence here did the job," said Corporal Brian Essex, 22, of Richmond, Texas.
From early morning marines sat by on packing cases, playing cards, reading and waiting for their final orders to pull out of the airport base for the operation that never was.
Razor wire that had surrounded the camp was neatly coiled again to be used elswhere.

Confined to the airport or to hotels in Brazzaville, and with a strict ban on alcoholic drink, the marines spent their time training in the tropical oven and for some, disappointment that they never got across the river was hard to hide.
The closest any of the marines got to fighting was the sound of distant shelling and small arms fire and the night-time sight of tracer bullets, five km (three miles) across the churning Zaire river.

"If the bad is going to go down then that's what we're psyched up for, so when it doesn't happen it's a letdown," said Sergeant Stacey Judge of Brooklyn, N.Y., who spent his 26th birthday quietly at the air base, celebrating with dry rations and copious amounts of water.

"We have to wait until we get into the next port, that's when we get to celebrate," said Corporal Michael Simone of Winston-Sale, North Carolina, who missed a 21st birthday party for the watch over Zaire.

British troops are already on the way out, but those from France and Belgium, Zaire's former colonial power, have not yet been given orders to step down their forces. Portugal also has troops in Congo.
